script.opening: "Hi doc — quick one, I just want to book the prostate blood test, the PSA. A mate at work just got diagnosed with prostate cancer, completely out of the blue, and it’s shaken me up. So I figured I’d get the test, it comes back normal, and I can stop worrying. That’s how it works, right? Normal result means I’m in the clear?"

facts.text: He believes PSA is a binary "all-clear" test — normal = no cancer, raised = cancer. In reality PSA is non-specific: it can be raised by BPH, infection, recent ejaculation/exercise/catheter; it misses some cancers (false negatives) and finds indolent ones that may never harm him (over-diagnosis), leading to biopsy harms and over-treatment.

If asked: Black ethnicity (higher risk, earlier onset) — genuinely relevant and a legitimate part of the discussion. If asked about family: an uncle had prostate cancer "late in life" — a second-degree relative diagnosed at an older age, which adds little; no father or brother affected, and no known BRCA variant or family breast/ovarian cancer. No lower-urinary-tract symptoms.

HIDDEN AGENDA — beneath the breezy request is real anxiety triggered by his friend, and a deeper, unspoken fear: he is far more frightened of the consequences he’s heard about (biopsy, impotence, incontinence from treatment) than he lets on, and is hoping a quick normal test lets him avoid all of that. He needs the informed-choice conversation, not a reflex blood form OR a refusal.

If reached: what he actually wants is to not die like nothing was done, AND to not be harmed by tests/treatment he didn’t understand. He needs the pros and cons to make HIS choice, with his ethnicity weighted in.

Officially: a PSA test as an all-clear. What he needs: a balanced informed-choice discussion (PSA is his right to request after counselling; it is not a simple all-clear), his elevated risk acknowledged, and support to make an informed decision rather than a reflex test or a paternalistic no.

ice.ideas: PSA is a simple all-clear test — a normal result means he definitely doesn’t have prostate cancer.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — anxiety triggered by a colleague’s diagnosis, plus an unspoken fear of the downstream harms (biopsy, impotence, incontinence) he’s hoping a quick normal test lets him sidestep.
ice.expectations: To be given the test as reassurance. What he needs: a balanced informed-choice conversation, his higher (Black-ethnicity) risk acknowledged, and a decision that is genuinely his.

cues: "Normal means I’m in the clear, right?" — the misconception to correct; PSA is not a binary all-clear.
Triggered by a colleague’s diagnosis — anxiety, not a considered screening decision; address the fear.
If risk factors emerge (Black ethnicity, family history) — these genuinely shift the conversation and must be weighted.

checkpoints.text: Corrects the core misconception with balance: PSA is NOT a simple all-clear — it is non-specific (raised by BPH, infection, ejaculation, exercise), misses some cancers (false negatives), and detects indolent cancers (over-diagnosis) that can lead to biopsy harms and over-treatment

Delivers a genuine INFORMED-CHOICE discussion: the benefits (may detect significant cancer earlier) and harms (false positives, biopsy complications, over-diagnosis/over-treatment, anxiety) — supporting his right to choose rather than reflexively testing or refusing

Elicits and WEIGHTS his risk factors accurately: Black ethnicity (higher and earlier risk) is a legitimate part of the individual discussion; the uncle is a second-degree relative diagnosed late, which adds little — the family history that matters is a father or brother with prostate cancer, or a BRCA variant/family breast or ovarian cancer; and he is in the eligible age group (50 or over) to request PSA after counselling under the Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme. men with a BRCA2 variant are high risk and have targeted surveillance through specialist or genetics pathways, not population screening

Explains what happens around a test properly: avoid ejaculation/vigorous exercise/recent UTI before testing; defer for 6 weeks after a urinary infection or prostate biopsy; that a raised result leads to repeat testing and multiparametric MRI before any biopsy (NICE NG131); and that asymptomatic men aged 50 or over can request PSA in primary care after an informed discussion (UKHSA Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme)

Screens briefly for symptoms and red flags (LUTS, haematuria, bone pain, weight loss) that would change the pathway from informed choice to a symptomatic assessment (NICE NG12: consider PSA and DRE in men with lower urinary tract symptoms, erectile dysfunction or visible haematuria; with symptoms, consider a suspected cancer referral if PSA is above the age-specific threshold — above 3.5 micrograms/L at 50–59) — and acts accordingly if present
Hears the anxiety and the unspoken fear of treatment harms beneath the request; addresses the colleague’s diagnosis and the fear directly rather than processing a blood form
Respects autonomy: supports him to make HIS decision (test or not) with the facts, rather than imposing a view; checks understanding and what matters to him

Safety-nets and follows up: if he tests, how and when results are discussed and the plan for a raised value; if he defers, what symptoms should prompt return; documents the informed-choice discussion and arranges appropriate follow-up

worked.txt: "I’m really sorry about your colleague — that kind of news lands hard, and wanting to do something sensible in response is completely understandable. Let’s make sure what we do is genuinely useful to you. Can I be straight about what the PSA test actually is, because it’s a bit different from how most people picture it?"

"It’s not a simple ‘all-clear’ test, much as I wish it were. The PSA can be up for harmless reasons — an enlarged prostate, a recent infection, even cycling or sex beforehand. And it cuts both ways: it can be normal when there IS a cancer, and it can flag slow-growing cancers that would never have troubled you — which then leads to biopsies and treatments that carry their own risks. So a normal result wouldn’t quite mean ‘in the clear’."

"That said, one thing genuinely matters for you specifically. You’re of Black ethnicity, which carries a higher and earlier risk of prostate cancer. Your uncle’s diagnosis late in life adds less than a father or brother would — can I check nobody closer has had it, or breast or ovarian cancer? Your background makes it very reasonable to test — you’re absolutely entitled to the PSA after a chat like this, from 50. I’m not talking you out of it; I’m making sure it’s your informed choice."

"Can I gently ask — part of what I hear is hoping a quick normal test means you avoid all the scary stuff you’ve heard about, the biopsies, the effects on waterworks and sex life. Is that fair? … That’s a very honest worry, and worth talking through, because understanding the path AFTER a raised result is part of deciding whether to test."

"So here are your options, and either is reasonable. We do the PSA now, knowing how to interpret it and what a raised number would mean next — repeat test, maybe an MRI before any biopsy. Or you take a week to weigh it up with what we’ve discussed. Given your background, if you want the test, I’m happy to do it. What feels right to you?"

"If we test: no sex or hard exercise for 48 hours first, and tell me if you’ve had any waterworks trouble, blood in the urine, or bone pain — those change things. We’ll go through the result together, and I won’t leave you to interpret a number alone. If you defer, come back any time, and definitely if any of those symptoms appear. Either way, you’re making the decision with the full picture now — that’s the point."

f.learning: A PSA request is an informed-choice consultation, not a reflex blood form or a paternalistic refusal. The core task is correcting the "all-clear" misconception with balance: PSA is non-specific (raised by BPH, infection, ejaculation, exercise), yields false negatives, and over-diagnoses indolent cancers, leading to biopsy harms and over-treatment — so a normal result is not "in the clear". The genuine informed-choice discussion lays out benefits and harms and supports the man’s right to decide; asymptomatic eligible men can request PSA after counselling. Risk factors must be weighted honestly — Black ethnicity (higher, earlier risk) is a legitimate part of the discussion; an uncle is a second-degree relative and adds little, whereas a father or brother, or a BRCA variant, would matter. BRCA2 carriers are high risk and have targeted surveillance through specialist or genetics pathways, not population screening; the Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme applies from 50. The examinable hidden agenda is anxiety triggered by a colleague’s diagnosis plus an unspoken fear of downstream treatment harms he hopes a quick normal test will let him avoid; surface and address it. Screen briefly for symptoms/red flags that would convert this to a symptomatic NICE NG12 pathway, give pre-test practicalities, and safety-net the result and follow-up.

knowledge.guideline: UKHSA Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme (GOV.UK) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · UK NSC (no population prostate screening programme) · NICE NG131 (2019, updated 2021)
knowledge.summary: An asymptomatic man aged 50 or over can have a PSA test after a balanced discussion. Help him make an informed choice — neither refuse nor reflexively test — and give real weight to his higher risk as a Black man.

points.t: Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme: an asymptomatic man aged 50 or over who asks about PSA should be given balanced information on benefits and harms and can then choose to be tested. There is no national population screening programme.

There is no population PSA screening programme. Follow the current Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme / NHS prostate pathway, using age-specific PSA thresholds and local referral criteria. Men with a BRCA2 variant are at high risk: targeted surveillance is arranged through specialist or clinical genetics pathways, not population screening. Black men are also at higher risk — a legitimate part of an individual discussion.

points.h: What PSA can and cannot do
points.t: PSA rises with benign enlargement, infection, recent ejaculation and vigorous exercise. It can be normal with a significant cancer and can detect slow-growing cancers that would never cause harm, leading to biopsy and treatment side effects. A normal result is not an all-clear.
Programme advice: no ejaculation or vigorous exercise for 48 hours beforehand, and defer for 6 weeks after a urinary infection or a prostate biopsy.

For an asymptomatic man tested under the Programme, a PSA of 3.0 micrograms/L or more (age 50 to 69) prompts urological referral. The NICE NG12 age-specific thresholds (for 50–59 years, above 3.5 micrograms/L) apply to symptomatic men. NICE NG131: multiparametric MRI is the first-line investigation for suspected localised prostate cancer, before any biopsy; active surveillance is an option for low-risk disease.

NICE NG12: consider PSA and digital rectal examination in men with lower urinary tract symptoms, erectile dysfunction or visible haematuria. Bone pain, weight loss or a hard irregular prostate move this from informed choice to a symptomatic assessment.

dg.d: Asked what prompted the request before discussing the test; let him explain the colleague’s diagnosis.
Impact of the colleague’s illness, who supports him, and what matters to him about possible treatment effects.
Symptom screen; informed-choice PSA with pre-test advice (48 hours, 6 weeks after infection); DRE if symptoms arise.
Asymptomatic informed choice versus symptomatic presentation; benign causes of a raised PSA.
Asked about LUTS, haematuria, erectile dysfunction, bone pain and weight loss that would change the pathway (NICE NG12).
Summarised: asymptomatic man at higher-than-average risk, eligible for PSA after counselling; no symptoms needing urgent assessment.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Balanced benefits and harms; his choice respected; explained MRI-first pathway (NICE NG131) and active surveillance if a raised result.
Weighed Black ethnicity and family history; asked about BRCA-pattern cancers; explained second-degree history carries less weight than first-degree.
Result given personally, plan for a raised or normal value, symptom safety-net, and informed choice documented.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “normal means I’m clear” and “biopsies and all that” and explored the fear of treatment harms.
Idea (PSA is an all-clear); concern (cancer, and sexual and urinary side effects of treatment); expectation (a quick normal test).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — anxiety triggered by a colleague’s diagnosis, plus an unspoken fear of the downstream harms (biopsy, impotence, incontinence) he’s hoping a quick normal test lets him sidestep — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Trevor, I’m Dr Lee. You’d like to talk about a PSA test — tell me what’s brought this up now.
model.why: Open question about the trigger rather than processing the request

model.text: A mate at work just got diagnosed with prostate cancer, out of nowhere. Shook me up. So I thought I’d get the test, it comes back normal, and I can stop worrying. Normal means I’m in the clear, right?

I’m sorry about your colleague — that’s a shock. I’m happy to talk about the test, and I want to give you a straight answer on what “normal” means. First, can I ask a few questions about you, then we’ll go through the pros and cons and you can decide. Okay?
model.why: Acknowledges the trigger and sets an informed-choice agenda

model.text: Sure. I thought it was just a blood test.
Any trouble with your waterworks — getting up at night, a weak stream, rushing to the loo, or any blood in your urine?
model.why: Screens for lower urinary tract symptoms and haematuria

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Any problems with erections, pain in your bones or back, or weight loss you can’t explain?
model.why: Screens for symptoms that would move this to a symptomatic pathway

model.text: No. I feel fine. That’s the scary bit about my mate — he felt fine too.
Has anyone in your family had prostate cancer, or breast or ovarian cancer?
model.why: Asks about family history, including BRCA-type patterns

model.text: My uncle had it, late in life. Nothing else I know of.
Thank you. One more thing that matters — prostate cancer is more common in Black men, and tends to come on a bit earlier. That’s relevant for you, and I’ll come back to it.
model.why: Recognises Black ethnicity as a genuine risk factor

model.text: I’d heard something like that.
When you picture having the test, what are you hoping it does for you?
Settles it. Normal, done. I don’t want to go down the road of biopsies and all that.
Tell me more about “all that” — what have you heard?
model.why: Follows the cue towards the hidden fear

model.text: Well… my mate’s talking about surgery. And people say you end up not able to — you know — in the bedroom. Or wearing pads. That frightens me more than anything, if I’m honest.
That’s a really honest thing to say, and it’s actually central to this decision. Because the test can start you down that road, understanding it is part of choosing whether to have it.
model.why: Validates the fear and links it to the decision

model.text: So here’s the honest picture. The PSA is useful, but it isn’t an all-clear. It can be raised by harmless things — a large prostate, an infection, even sex or a long bike ride. It can be normal even when there is a cancer. And sometimes it finds slow-growing cancers that would never have harmed you.
model.why: Corrects the all-clear belief with balance

model.text: So what’s the point then?

The point is it can find a significant cancer earlier, when it’s more treatable. For a man of your background, with an uncle affected, that benefit counts for more. You’re entitled to the test, and I’d support you having it if that’s your choice.
model.why: Presents benefits honestly and weighs his individual risk

model.text: And if it comes back high?

Then we’d likely repeat it, and refer you to the specialists. These days the next step is usually an MRI scan, and many men don’t need a biopsy at all. If a low-risk cancer is found, often the choice is careful monitoring rather than surgery — so a raised result doesn’t automatically mean the treatments you’re worried about.
model.why: Explains the downstream pathway (MRI first, active surveillance)

model.text: That’s not what I thought. That’s better, actually.

So there are two reasonable options. Have the test now, knowing what it can and can’t tell you. Or take some time, read the leaflet I’ll send, and decide later. There’s no wrong answer. What feels right to you?
I think I want it. I’d rather know. But I get now it’s not a yes or no.

That’s a well-thought-through choice. A couple of practical points: no sex and no hard exercise for 48 hours before the blood test, and if you get a urine infection, we’d wait six weeks. I’ll book it for next week.
Right. 48 hours. Got it.

I’ll go through the result with you myself, not just a text. If it’s normal, we’ll talk about when it might be worth repeating. And whatever the result, if you ever notice waterworks changes, blood in your urine, bone pain or weight loss, come and see us.
model.why: Result ownership, follow-up and symptom safety-net

model.text: Okay. Thanks for not just handing me a form.
Before you go — if someone at home asks what the test tells you, what will you say?
That it’s a clue, not an answer. Normal doesn’t mean definitely clear, high doesn’t mean definitely cancer, and the next step is a scan.
Spot on. I’ll record that we’ve talked it through and that it’s your decision. Take care, Trevor.
model.why: Affirms his decision and documents informed choice

social.t: A colleague’s sudden diagnosis has made the risk personal. Acknowledge it — decisions made in fear can be regretted either way.
Fear of erectile dysfunction and incontinence is often the real barrier for men considering PSA; raise it sensitively.

legal.t: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board (2015): patients must be told about material risks and reasonable alternatives. For PSA, that includes false results, overdiagnosis and the option not to test.

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): share information in a balanced way, find out what matters to the patient, and respect his choice. Document the discussion and his decision.
Black men have a higher risk of prostate cancer and may be less likely to seek testing. Discussing that risk openly is good care, not stereotyping.

community.t: Programme patient information leaflet on the PSA test; Prostate Cancer UK information and specialist nurse helpline.

redFlags: Lower urinary tract symptoms, erectile dysfunction or visible haematuria — consider PSA and DRE (NICE NG12)
Bone pain, back pain, weight loss or fatigue — possible advanced disease
Family history of prostate cancer in a first-degree relative, or breast or ovarian cancer suggesting a BRCA variant
psychosocial: The colleague’s diagnosis and how it has affected him
What sexual and urinary function mean to him
How he prefers to make decisions and who he talks to
ice: Idea: “PSA is a simple test — normal means I’m in the clear.”
Concern: cancer like his colleague, and the side effects of biopsy and treatment
Expectation: a quick blood test with a normal result

playbook.diagnosis: Asymptomatic 55-year-old Black man requesting PSA after a colleague’s diagnosis; higher-than-average risk from ethnicity, with a second-degree family history. No symptoms suggesting a symptomatic pathway. Eligible for PSA after an informed-choice discussion.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The PSA test is like a smoke alarm that sometimes goes off when there’s only toast burning, and occasionally stays quiet when there is a fire. It’s still useful — but you need to know that before you decide to install it.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for a quick all-clear, and underneath I think you’re as worried about the treatments as the cancer itself. Let’s look at both, so whatever you choose, you choose it knowing the full picture.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the colleague’s illness; talk openly about sexual and urinary side effects and how the modern pathway reduces unnecessary treatment.
sharedPlan: Balanced discussion of benefits and harms; his decision respected either way
If testing: no ejaculation or vigorous exercise for 48 hours, defer 6 weeks after a UTI
Raised result for age: repeat and refer (NICE NG12); MRI before biopsy (NICE NG131)
safetyNet: GP discusses the result personally and agrees when to consider repeating it
Return if urinary symptoms, blood in the urine, erectile problems, bone pain or weight loss

pitfalls.intro: Candidates fail this station at either extreme: the reflex blood form or the paternalistic refusal. The marks sit in the balanced conversation, the weighting of his risk, and the fear of treatment he does not volunteer.

items.fail: Agreeing that a normal PSA means he is in the clear.
items.why: PSA misses some significant cancers; false reassurance is a clinical error.
items.fix: “A normal result is reassuring but not a guarantee.”

items.fail: Declining the test because “there’s no screening programme”.
items.why: The risk management programme allows asymptomatic men aged 50 or over to choose PSA after counselling; refusal is outdated and paternalistic.
items.fix: Explain there is no population screening, then offer the test as his informed choice.

items.fail: No symptom screen before treating it as an informed-choice request.
items.why: LUTS, ED, haematuria or bone pain change the pathway under NICE NG12.
items.fix: Four quick questions: waterworks, blood in the urine, erections, bone pain or weight loss.

items.fail: Ignoring his ethnicity, or overstating a second-degree family history.
items.why: Black ethnicity is a genuine risk factor; an uncle’s late-life cancer adds little compared with a father or brother.
items.fix: Weigh both accurately and say so.

items.fail: Reciting benefits and harms as a list without finding out what worries him.
items.why: Feedback: “information not tailored to the patient’s concerns”. His fear of impotence and incontinence is what drives the decision.
items.fix: Ask what he has heard about biopsies and treatment, then explain MRI-first and active surveillance.

items.fail: No pre-test advice and no plan for who gives the result.
items.why: Spuriously raised results and unexplained numbers create harm and anxiety.
items.fix: 48 hours without ejaculation or hard exercise; “I’ll go through the result with you myself.”

timeMap.d: Ask what prompted it. Name that you’ll explain what “normal” really means and that the decision is his.
LUTS, haematuria, ED, bone pain, weight loss; family history including breast or ovarian cancer; acknowledge ethnicity as a real risk factor.
What does he hope the test does? What has he heard about biopsies and treatment? The fear of harms is the hidden agenda.
Not an all-clear; false positives and negatives; overdiagnosis; the MRI-first pathway and active surveillance. Weigh his risk. Offer the choice.
Pre-test advice if testing, personal result review, symptom safety-net, document informed choice. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Hands over a blood form with no discussion, or refuses the test as “not recommended”; confirms that normal means clear; ignores his ethnicity; no symptom screen; no plan for the result.
wordPics.pass: Explains PSA is not an all-clear and gives the main benefits and harms; screens for symptoms; recognises higher risk in Black men; respects his decision; gives pre-test advice and arranges results.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: surfaces the fear of impotence and incontinence and answers it with the MRI-first pathway and active surveillance; weighs family history accurately; offers time to decide as a real option; teach-back shows he understands a normal result is not a guarantee.

avoid.dont: “Sure, I’ll add it to your bloods.”
avoid.instead: “Happy to — can I first explain what the result can and can’t tell you, so it’s a decision you’re comfortable with?”
avoid.why: Testing without counselling fails the informed-choice task.

avoid.dont: “We don’t recommend PSA screening, so I’d rather not.”
avoid.instead: “There’s no national screening, but you’re entitled to the test after we’ve talked it through — and your background makes that discussion more relevant.”
avoid.why: Refusing an eligible man is paternalistic and wrong under the risk management programme.

avoid.dont: “If it’s normal, you’ve got nothing to worry about.”
avoid.instead: “A normal result is reassuring, but it isn’t a guarantee — so tell us if symptoms ever appear.”
avoid.why: False reassurance is the exact misconception this station tests.

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s not what I thought. That’s better, actually.

So there are two reasonable options. Have the test now, knowing what it can and can’t tell you. Or take some time, read the leaflet I’ll send, and decide later. There’s no wrong answer. What feels right to you?
I think I want it. I’d rather know. But I get now it’s not a yes or no.

That’s a well-thought-through choice. A couple of practical points: no sex and no hard exercise for 48 hours before the blood test, and if you get a urine infection, we’d wait six weeks. I’ll book it for next week.
Right. 48 hours. Got it.

I’ll go through the result with you myself, not just a text. If it’s normal, we’ll talk about when it might be worth repeating. And whatever the result, if you ever notice waterworks changes, blood in your urine, bone pain or weight loss, come and see us.
SCA_MODELS.why: Result ownership, follow-up and symptom safety-net

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Thanks for not just handing me a form.
Before you go — if someone at home asks what the test tells you, what will you say?
That it’s a clue, not an answer. Normal doesn’t mean definitely clear, high doesn’t mean definitely cancer, and the next step is a scan.
Spot on. I’ll record that we’ve talked it through and that it’s your decision. Take care, Trevor.
SCA_MODELS.why: Affirms his decision and documents informed choice

SCA_STEM.name: Trevor Hammond
SCA_STEM.recent: No PSA on record. Ethnicity recorded as Black. No urinary symptoms documented.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment: “wants to book a PSA blood test”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: UKHSA Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme (GOV.UK) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · UK NSC (no population prostate screening programme) · NICE NG131 (2019, updated 2021)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: An asymptomatic man aged 50 or over can have a PSA test after a balanced discussion. Help him make an informed choice — neither refuse nor reflexively test — and give real weight to his higher risk as a Black man.

points.t: Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme: an asymptomatic man aged 50 or over who asks about PSA should be given balanced information on benefits and harms and can then choose to be tested. There is no national population screening programme.

There is no population PSA screening programme. Follow the current Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme / NHS prostate pathway, using age-specific PSA thresholds and local referral criteria. Men with a BRCA2 variant are at high risk: targeted surveillance is arranged through specialist or clinical genetics pathways, not population screening. Black men are also at higher risk — a legitimate part of an individual discussion.

points.h: What PSA can and cannot do
points.t: PSA rises with benign enlargement, infection, recent ejaculation and vigorous exercise. It can be normal with a significant cancer and can detect slow-growing cancers that would never cause harm, leading to biopsy and treatment side effects. A normal result is not an all-clear.
Programme advice: no ejaculation or vigorous exercise for 48 hours beforehand, and defer for 6 weeks after a urinary infection or a prostate biopsy.

For an asymptomatic man tested under the Programme, a PSA of 3.0 micrograms/L or more (age 50 to 69) prompts urological referral. The NICE NG12 age-specific thresholds (for 50–59 years, above 3.5 micrograms/L) apply to symptomatic men. NICE NG131: multiparametric MRI is the first-line investigation for suspected localised prostate cancer, before any biopsy; active surveillance is an option for low-risk disease.

NICE NG12: consider PSA and digital rectal examination in men with lower urinary tract symptoms, erectile dysfunction or visible haematuria. Bone pain, weight loss or a hard irregular prostate move this from informed choice to a symptomatic assessment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Asked what prompted the request before discussing the test; let him explain the colleague’s diagnosis.
Impact of the colleague’s illness, who supports him, and what matters to him about possible treatment effects.
Picked up “normal means I’m clear” and “biopsies and all that” and explored the fear of treatment harms.
Idea (PSA is an all-clear); concern (cancer, and sexual and urinary side effects of treatment); expectation (a quick normal test).
Symptom screen; informed-choice PSA with pre-test advice (48 hours, 6 weeks after infection); DRE if symptoms arise.
Asymptomatic informed choice versus symptomatic presentation; benign causes of a raised PSA.
Asked about LUTS, haematuria, erectile dysfunction, bone pain and weight loss that would change the pathway (NICE NG12).
Summarised: asymptomatic man at higher-than-average risk, eligible for PSA after counselling; no symptoms needing urgent assessment.
Balanced benefits and harms; his choice respected; explained MRI-first pathway (NICE NG131) and active surveillance if a raised result.
Weighed Black ethnicity and family history; asked about BRCA-pattern cancers; explained second-degree history carries less weight than first-degree.
Result given personally, plan for a raised or normal value, symptom safety-net, and informed choice documented.

social.t: A colleague’s sudden diagnosis has made the risk personal. Acknowledge it — decisions made in fear can be regretted either way.
Fear of erectile dysfunction and incontinence is often the real barrier for men considering PSA; raise it sensitively.

legal.t: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board (2015): patients must be told about material risks and reasonable alternatives. For PSA, that includes false results, overdiagnosis and the option not to test.

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): share information in a balanced way, find out what matters to the patient, and respect his choice. Document the discussion and his decision.
Black men have a higher risk of prostate cancer and may be less likely to seek testing. Discussing that risk openly is good care, not stereotyping.

community.t: Programme patient information leaflet on the PSA test; Prostate Cancer UK information and specialist nurse helpline.

redFlags: Lower urinary tract symptoms, erectile dysfunction or visible haematuria — consider PSA and DRE (NICE NG12)
Bone pain, back pain, weight loss or fatigue — possible advanced disease
Family history of prostate cancer in a first-degree relative, or breast or ovarian cancer suggesting a BRCA variant
psychosocial: The colleague’s diagnosis and how it has affected him
What sexual and urinary function mean to him
How he prefers to make decisions and who he talks to
ice: Idea: “PSA is a simple test — normal means I’m in the clear.”
Concern: cancer like his colleague, and the side effects of biopsy and treatment
Expectation: a quick blood test with a normal result

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Asymptomatic 55-year-old Black man requesting PSA after a colleague’s diagnosis; higher-than-average risk from ethnicity, with a second-degree family history. No symptoms suggesting a symptomatic pathway. Eligible for PSA after an informed-choice discussion.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The PSA test is like a smoke alarm that sometimes goes off when there’s only toast burning, and occasionally stays quiet when there is a fire. It’s still useful — but you need to know that before you decide to install it.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for a quick all-clear, and underneath I think you’re as worried about the treatments as the cancer itself. Let’s look at both, so whatever you choose, you choose it knowing the full picture.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the colleague’s illness; talk openly about sexual and urinary side effects and how the modern pathway reduces unnecessary treatment.
sharedPlan: Balanced discussion of benefits and harms; his decision respected either way
If testing: no ejaculation or vigorous exercise for 48 hours, defer 6 weeks after a UTI
Raised result for age: repeat and refer (NICE NG12); MRI before biopsy (NICE NG131)
safetyNet: GP discusses the result personally and agrees when to consider repeating it
Return if urinary symptoms, blood in the urine, erectile problems, bone pain or weight loss

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Candidates fail this station at either extreme: the reflex blood form or the paternalistic refusal. The marks sit in the balanced conversation, the weighting of his risk, and the fear of treatment he does not volunteer.

items.fail: Agreeing that a normal PSA means he is in the clear.
items.why: PSA misses some significant cancers; false reassurance is a clinical error.
items.fix: “A normal result is reassuring but not a guarantee.”

items.fail: Declining the test because “there’s no screening programme”.
items.why: The risk management programme allows asymptomatic men aged 50 or over to choose PSA after counselling; refusal is outdated and paternalistic.
items.fix: Explain there is no population screening, then offer the test as his informed choice.

items.fail: No symptom screen before treating it as an informed-choice request.
items.why: LUTS, ED, haematuria or bone pain change the pathway under NICE NG12.
items.fix: Four quick questions: waterworks, blood in the urine, erections, bone pain or weight loss.

items.fail: Ignoring his ethnicity, or overstating a second-degree family history.
items.why: Black ethnicity is a genuine risk factor; an uncle’s late-life cancer adds little compared with a father or brother.
items.fix: Weigh both accurately and say so.

items.fail: Reciting benefits and harms as a list without finding out what worries him.
items.why: Feedback: “information not tailored to the patient’s concerns”. His fear of impotence and incontinence is what drives the decision.
items.fix: Ask what he has heard about biopsies and treatment, then explain MRI-first and active surveillance.

items.fail: No pre-test advice and no plan for who gives the result.
items.why: Spuriously raised results and unexplained numbers create harm and anxiety.
items.fix: 48 hours without ejaculation or hard exercise; “I’ll go through the result with you myself.”
